items.title: Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes and deep in Amazon
items.summary:
CUSCO, Peru (AP) — The plight of Indigenous peoples and the protection of the Amazon take center stage Sunday as Pope Leo XIV travels across Peru to visit communities high in the Andes and deep in the rainforest.

On the penultimate day of his visit to his adopted homeland, Leo is expected to echo Pope Francis, emphasizing Catholic teaching that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.

He travels first to Cusco, the former capital of the Inca empire, before flying to the Amazonian city of Pucallpa, where illegal mining, deforestation and threats to Indigenous communities will be central concerns.

“The church in Peru perceives the continuity of his commitment to accompany Indigenous peoples in the defense of life and the care of the territory, which is increasingly threatened by deforestation and illegal mining,” Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto, president of the Amazon bishops conference, told The Associated Press.

“Leo is clearing the path laid out” by Francis on environmental protection and human rights, Barreto said. He added that the pope would hear about violence affecting children and young people.

From the Andes to the Amazon 

The visit to Cusco, 3,400 meters (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, will test the stamina of the pope, who is recovering from lung cancer surgery.

His schedule begins at the historic Sacsayhuamán fortress, where he will speak about local religious devotion. In the Plaza de Armas, he will present a shroud from the Holy See for the image of the Lord of the Earthquakes, a focus of devotion in a country prone to…
items.t: Pope crosses Peru in finale of trip home to visit flock high in Andes and deep in Amazon

items.title: One of the secrets to a happy marriage
items.summary:
Nothing makes me feel more loved than when my wife makes me a cup of coffee. It’s a small gesture. She’s already making coffee for herself but thinks to make enough for me and share it. We’ve been married for almost 25 years now and she knows what I like. I like coffee. As I said, it’s a small thing, a simple gesture, but it isn’t really about the drink; it’s an act of kindness that unveils a hugely important reason that our marriage continues to thrive — she’s thinking of me even within the ordinary details of her life. There’s room for me. Not only when she wants to make a grand romantic gesture, but also she carries me with her wherever she goes. The fact that she thinks about me at all and finds little ways to express it means everything. In a long-term relationship, it’s the small things that matter most. The Read More… 

One of the secrets to a happy marriage

items.title: How do we face uncertainty without allowing it to overwhelm us? This Islamic teaching shows us the way
items.summary:
For generations of Muslims, tawakkul has been an essential part of faith – making a sincere effort while recognising the limits of human control

I once asked an elderly naan seller on the streets of Kabul how he was managing to make a living. It was almost midday and he had not sold a single naan. What would he take home, I asked. “Tawakkul ba Khuda,” he replied.

He had a long silver beard, deep brown eyes and a beautiful smile. As a frontline journalist covering the Afghan war, I had heard those words many times before. From a young woman trying to establish a clothing business in the middle of the conflict, to a military commander confronting a deadly insurgency, to a school student preparing for the long and uncertain journey towards a university degree, the expression seemed to surface wherever hope and hardship met.

Continue reading...
items.t: How do we face uncertainty without allowing it to overwhelm us? This Islamic teaching shows us the way

items.title: The reason we barely know who built the Gothic cathedrals
items.summary:
Walk into Chartres Cathedral and you are surrounded, by any measure, by one of the supreme achievements of human civilization. The light through the rose windows, the geometry of the vaulting, the carved figures on the Royal Portal, each one a minor miracle of stone. The whole building went up in roughly 26 years, after a fire destroyed the earlier structure in 1194 — an extraordinary speed for a structure of that complexity and scale. We know who ordered it built. Bishop Renaud de Mousson commissioned the reconstruction. The donors who funded the stained glass are also documented: the bakers, the fur merchants, the drapers, each guild immortalized in a panel depicting their trade alongside the saint they venerated. Their names and professions are there in the glass, permanent advertisements for piety and money. The people who actually built it — the master mason who solved the structural problems, the imagiers who carved the portal Read More… 

The reason we barely know who built the Gothic cathedrals

items.summary:

Initially he served in a variety of capacities before being named the Bishop of Chiclayo in 2015. Pope Leo spent so much time in the country that he was able to become a naturalized citizen of Peru. The country holds a special place in his heart and is his “second home.” However Pope Leo, as Fr. items.title: American Carlo Acutis? Meet Francisco Fredrickson
items.summary:
When Laura Fredrickson, a mother of four from Virginia, began reading My Son Carlo — a memoir by Antonia Salzano Acutis, mother of St. Carlo Acutis — she kept putting down the book in shock. “It got a little creepy there for a bit!” she told Aleteia. “Whenever I would start reading it, I would need to stop because I would bump into something that had happened to my family, in almost exactly the same way.” Fredrickson’s oldest child, Francisco, died on December 5, 2024. He was barely nine years old, and he had spent the last 18 months of his life fighting diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG), a rare and incurable form of brain cancer.  Yet in his short time on earth, her son lived no ordinary life. Even as he suffered increasing pain and loss of abilities, little Francisco Fredrickson never lost his joyful trust in God and hope in the goodness of Heaven. Read More…

On the fourth day of his visit to Peru, during a Mass attended by 20,000 people, he expressed his support for the Andean communities and called for a fairer distribution of wealth. After visiting Chiclayo Cathedral the day after his arrival in the northern city, the Pope took a helicopter to travel the 100 km (some 60 miles) to the rural area of Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, at an altitude of 2,000 meters (6,500 feet). items.title: Pope’s visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru
items.summary:
ZAÑA, Peru — When Susana Baca, the Latin Grammy-winning Afro-Peruvian singer, serenaded Pope Leo XIV upon his arrival in Peru, it was a sign that the visit would provide an unparalleled spotlight on the culture that grew out of the African slave trade to this country.

Baca, arguably the best-known Afro-Peruvian musician, was also Peru’s first Black Cabinet minister and became a leading figure in the campaign to end the discrimination that has long made second-class citizens of Black Peruvians and Peru’s Indigenous peoples.

The U.S.-born Leo, whose own family tree includes enslaved people and slave owners, is expected to highlight Peru’s African-descended community when he visits the hub of Afro-Peruvian culture on Saturday in the city of Zaña.

Leo will lead a prayer meeting at the sanctuary of St. Turibius of Mogrovejo in Zaña, where he often went to pray while bishop of nearby Chiclayo.

In the 16th century, Mogrovejo was the first archbishop of Lima. He defended the rights of Indigenous and enslaved people and was known for having confirmed St. Martin de Porres, the first Black saint of the Americas and the patron saint of racial harmony, social justice and people of multiracial backgrounds.

The pope has already apologized for slavery 

In his first encyclical, “Magnificent Humanity,” Leo made a sweeping apology for the role of past popes in legitimizing slavery in the Americas and failing to condemn it for centuries. It was a reference to the series of 15th-century directives from the Vatican that authorized European sovereigns to conquer Africa and the Americas and…
items.t: Pope’s visit to hub of Afro-Peruvian community casts spotlight on African slave trade to Peru

items.title: Huge crowds and low vaccination rates raise measles alarms as Pope Leo XIV visits South America
items.summary:
While millions of Catholics gather to catch a glimpse of Pope Leo XIV in South America, health authorities are watching for a different kind of visitor: Measles.

Cases are already surging in the region this year and mass gatherings provide an opportunity for one of the world’s most contagious viruses to spread further.

The Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO, and officials in Uruguay, Argentina and Peru have been preparing for potential problems to different degrees for months, including mounting vaccination campaigns and increasing surveillance to try to limit spread.

Uruguay, where thousands of people attended a prayer vigil and a Mass celebrated by Leo, implemented a nationwide intensified surveillance monitoring period until Nov. 29, three weeks after Leo’s departure from the country, according to Nataly Rodriguez, director of epidemiology at Uruguay’s health ministry. Uruguay has also taken steps to boost its vaccination rate to among the highest in the region.

“As a preventive strategy, the ministry has been emphasizing the importance of keeping vaccination schedules up to date,” Rodriguez said.

The Nov. 6-17 trip to the continent where around 40 percent of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics live marks a return home for Leo, who spent two decades ministering in Peru as a missionary priest and then bishop.

Ahead of the visit, PAHO assessed the public health risk of measles in the context of the religious mass gatherings in South America as “very high.” That’s in part because there has been a nearly five-fold increase in cases between January and October…
items.t: Huge crowds and low vaccination rates raise measles alarms as Pope Leo XIV visits South America

Turkish footballer Semih Güler might have discovered the secret to winning matches. Forget complicated tactics, extra training sessions, or a rousing halftime team talk. Apparently, all he needs is his little daughter Defne cheering him on! And he has the results to prove it. The little girl has attended two of her dad’s matches, and his team has won both. Not a bad record for such a young supporter! But forget the victories, it’s a video of the Kayserispor defender holding Defne in his arms during a post-match interview that’s really stealing our hearts. items.summary:
In an increasingly digital world, Natural Womanhood has gone against the tide to offer a body literacy journal women can hold in their hands. The Natural Womanhood journal guides women (and even older teens!) to learn how to chart their menstrual cycles and to pay attention to what cues their bodies are giving them. In a culture that can speak negatively about periods and women’s health in general, this journal is part of a movement to show women the truth about how we are designed and to empower them in their health and lifestyle choices. Natural Womanhood Program Manager Ryane Gibbens says this project grew out of a need for more tools that promote body literacy. Natural Womanhood, which also has an extensive online magazine, runs Cycle Mindfulness Clubs at a number of universities. items.title: The discipline of hope: Why it isn’t optimism rebranded
items.summary:
We tend to treat hope as something that happens to us — a feeling that arrives or doesn’t, depending on circumstances. When things look good, we feel hopeful. When they look bad, the feeling drains away. On this account, hope is basically optimism rebranded: a disposition of the fortunate, the constitutionally sunny, the people who haven’t been paying attention to the news. Philosophical and theological traditions have a sharper account. Hope is a practice. It has to be learned. It can be lost through neglect and recovered through effort. It is, in the precise sense of the word, a discipline — something you do, something you sustain, something that makes demands on you in return for what it gives. Take Ernst Bloch. He was a German-Jewish philosopher who spent much of his life in exile — first from Nazi Germany, then, after a brief return, from an East German communist regime that found him too Read More…

items.title: Our Lady of Evangelization is the oldest Marian devotion in Peru
items.summary:
The Blessed Virgin Mary is held in high esteem in many South American countries and each has a particular Marian devotion that is widely beloved by the local people. In Peru, that devotion is Nuestra Señora de la Evangelización (Our Lady of Evangelization), who has been a large part of Peruvian devotional life since the 16th century. It is believed that this statue of the Blessed Virgin Mary was originally commissioned by Francisco Pizarro’s daughter, Francisca, around 1551, and was to be installed over the main altar of Peru’s cathedral. Furthermore, the first flowering rose in the region was said to have been placed in the statue’s hand by Fray Jerónimo de Loayza, the first bishop of Lima. Since then the statue has been connected to the original evangelization of Peru. It remains a vital devotional symbol for the continued evangelization of the country. St. John Paul II crowned the statue on February 1, 1985, Read More…

After a warm welcome at Chiclayo’s air base earlier that morning, Leo immediately made his way to the vast plain of Pampas de Pimentel, a broad sandy expanse a few kilometers outside the city. Before entering the sacristy, he completed a full circuit in the popemobile among the 500,000 people gathered there, according to local authorities, in an atmosphere of euphoria that persisted despite oppressive heat and the dust that hung over the dry terrain. items.title: As Leo XIV returns to Chiclayo, the city comes out to meet him
items.summary:
Leo XIV landed at the Teniente Coronel Pedro Ruiz Gallo airport shortly after 9 a.m., stepping off a LATAM Airlines A320 that had departed Lima’s Callao military base at dawn. What waited for him was, yet again, a homecoming: folk dancers in traditional dress waving white handkerchiefs, flags of Peru and the Vatican crossing in choreographed patterns, and former colleagues from the diocese waiting on the tarmac to embrace him. An estimated one million people lined the 14 kilometers of road between the airport and the Pampas de Pimentel esplanade, where the Mass was scheduled. The scenes echoed Lima two days earlier: hands extended toward the popemobile, streets thick with people who had traveled from across the region of Lambayeque to see the man who had been their bishop from 2015 to 2023. “Today, our father, our brother, and our friend returns home, to his land,” said Sister Karina, a religious of the diocese, told Read More…

items.title: Leo XIV and young people: What this South American tour is building
items.summary:
Something has been visible throughout Pope Leo XIV’s ongoing journey through Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru: the man is genuinely at ease with young people. Three countries, three youth vigils, and crowds that, taken together, number well over a million. In Montevideo, some 100,000 gathered at the Estadio Centenario on November 7 for a prayer vigil that seemed to set the tone for everything that followed. Leo spoke directly to the question of commitment — urging young people not to be afraid of “forever,” to consider marriage and family, to refuse mediocrity in their faith. “Christ did not call us to mediocrity,” he told them. “He called us to a new and full life like his own.” He also asked them, simply: “Be saints.” In Buenos Aires, three days later, the scale shifted dramatically. items.title: Why Pope Leo’s blue chasuble is one of the rarest vestments
items.summary:
While celebrating Mass in front of the Basilica of Our Lady of Lujan in Buenos Aires, Argentina, Pope Leo wore a striking sky-blue chasuble. The image of Our Lady of Lujan has that same color. It was a rare occurrence, as generally speaking, blue is not a liturgical color that can be worn at Mass. Officially priests can wear vestments that are primarily white (or gold), red, green, violet (or rose) and, in some cases, black. These vestments can have various trim colors, such as blue, but the vestment must be primarily one of the above colors. Yet, popes have given particular regions of the world the permission to wear blue vestments. Historically speaking Catholics in Spain (including many Spanish kings) were pivotal in promoting devotion to the Marian dogma of the Immaculate Conception. items.title: Papa Johns Peru renames itself “Johns” for Leo XIV’s visit

Papa Johns Peru temporarily rebranded itself as “Johns” — removing the word Papa from storefronts, illuminated signs, and all social media profiles across the country. Papa, of course, is the word for Pope in Spanish. The reasoning was straightforward, and stated with some humor on their social media channels: “Cuando León XIV está en el Perú, Papa solo hay uno.” When Leo XIV is in Peru, there is only one Pope. items.title: After his emotional return, Pope denounces ‘machismo’ in Peru and demands women be protected
items.summary:
LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Thursday denounced widespread “machismo” and violence against women in Peru, demanding that women be protected and respected as he set out marching orders for his beloved Peruvian church and people. 

After his emotional homecoming Wednesday, the Peruvian pope got down to business and turned to the challenges facing a church and country he knows well.

He called on the influential Catholic hierarchy to be models of unity and communion, and instructed Peruvian bishops to accompany their flocks and respond to victims of clergy sexual abuse with truth and justice.

But the 71-year-old pope also showed himself to be positively overjoyed to be home and as relaxed as he has been in public since his 2025 election.

Leo sang along enthusiastically as 40,000 people in Lima’s Plaza Mayor serenaded him with “Contigo Perú,” a famous song from Peru’s Pacific coast that celebrates national unity. He drew huge applause when he recited the lyrics of another famous Creole hymn, “Mi Perú.”

“It’s a blessing not only for us Chiclayans but for all of Peru,” said Ángel Esquives, a craftsman originally from Leo’s former diocese in Chiclayo who now lives in Lima. He said he left his home at 3 a.m. to go to the historic center and stand in line to get as close as possible to the pope.

items.t: After his emotional return, Pope denounces ‘machismo’ in Peru and demands women be protected

items.title: Pope tells Peru’s bishops to accompany their flocks and respond to abuse victims with truth, justice
items.summary:
LIMA, Peru (AP) — After his emotional homecoming, Pope Leo XIV got down to work Thursday telling Peru’s Catholic bishops to accompany their flocks as they face poverty and injustices, and respond to victims of clergy sexual abuse with truth, justice and amends.

Leo made it clear he knows the Peruvian church and people well in his opening events in Lima, identifying some of the biggest challenges facing them and calling the influential Catholic hierarchy especially to task to be models of unity and communion.

Peruvians turned out in droves to catch a glimpse of Leo, with crowds outside the church residence where he is staying and an even bigger gathering at the central Plaza Mayor where he had his first events Thursday. Leo thrilled them by looping around the plaza in his popemobile.

At every turn, Leo has been serenaded by a children’s choir belting out a catchy tune composed especially for his trip, accompanied by Andean flutes: “Papa León, hermano del camino, Papa León, sembrador de fraternidad.” (“Pope Leo, brother on the journey, Pope Leo, sower of brotherhood.”)

“It’s a blessing not only for us Chiclayans but for all of Peru,” said Ángel Esquives, a craftsman originally from Leo’s former diocese in Chiclayo who now lives in Lima. He said he left his home at 3 a.m. to go to the historic center and stand in line to get as close as possible to the pope.

items.title: German ambassador to Vatican says Pope Leo XIV wants to visit Germany
items.summary:
According to Germany’s ambassador to the Vatican, Pope Leo XIV intends to visit the central European country.

Bruno Kahl, 63, said to Colonge-based Catholic website, domradio.de , that it was too early to start planning the trip but Leo’s intentions were clear.

“On behalf of the Federal Government, I renewed the invitation previously extended by the Federal President and confirmed by the Federal Foreign Minister. The answer is already clear: he intends to come to Germany,” he said. 

“However, the exact sequence of his upcoming trips is not yet fully defined. He himself says he advised his predecessor to visit Germany and will, of course, heed that advice. It is still too early for concrete planning, though,” he added.

Crux Now ‘s request for comment from the Vatican press office was without immediate reply.

Kahl also said his impressions of the pope were very positive.

“I was very impressed,” Kahl said. “The Pope is approachable, open, straightforward, speaks in an uncomplicated, direct way, and makes you feel personally taken seriously,” he said. 

“He is very quick-witted, humorous, and therefore an exceptionally pleasant conversationalist,” he also said.

Kahl had previously been critical of the Vatican’s stance on the war between Russia and Ukraine, particularly during Pope Francis’ pontificate, but he was more approving of Leo’s view on the conflict.

“First, I need to correct that somewhat,” he said when asked about his previous comments. 

“Especially regarding the criticism of equidistance, there has been progress between the pontificate of Francis and that…
items.t: German ambassador to Vatican says Pope Leo XIV wants to visit Germany

items.title: ‘Christianophobia’ added to dictionary by Royal Spanish Academy
items.summary:
Spain’s royal language watchdog has officially added “Christianophobia” to its dictionary.

The Royal Spanish Academy (RAE) has added the term “Christianophobia” to the 24th edition of its official book of words in the Spanish language, defining Christianophobia as an “aversion towards Christianity, Christians or anything Christian.”

The word Islamophobia is already in the dictionary alongside antisemitism. 

The Spanish Association of Christian Lawyers, a group that began campaigning for the inclusion of the word in January this year, celebrated the news.

In a statement sent to Crux Now, Polonia Castellanos, president of the group, called it a “historic victory.”

“For us, this is a historic victory, not only for Spanish Christians but for all Spanish speakers. For far too long, hostility and attacks against Christians have been ignored or treated as a minor issue,” she said.

“We found it incomprehensible that the dictionary recognized terms such as Islamophobia and antisemitism, yet did not include a word that explicitly identifies hostility towards Christianity,” she added.

She explained that the organization’s campaign gathered 15,000 signatures in support, and that they formally requested that the RAE include the word in January this year.

“We have always maintained that what cannot be named is much harder to recognize and combat,” Castellanos said.

“The inclusion of Christianophobia will not put an end to attacks against Christians, but it represents a very important step towards raising awareness of this reality and demanding that it receive the same attention…
items.t: ‘Christianophobia’ added to dictionary by Royal Spanish Academy

items.title: Pope Leo returns to what is expected to be a national party in his second homeland of Peru
items.summary:
LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV arrived in his second homeland of Peru on Wednesday, returning to the place that he credits with teaching him how to be a pastor and where a nationwide party awaits to welcome their beloved “Padre Robert” home.

The visit to Peru marks the final leg of Leo’s three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that the former Robert Prevost spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. As a dual citizen of the United States and Peru, he’s the first pope from each country.

Leo’s charter plane touched down at a Lima-area air base, where he was being welcomed by President Keiko Fujimori.

The visit to Peru marks the final leg of Leo’s three-nation South America tour and its emotional highlight, given the more than two decades that the former Robert Prevost spent in Peru as a missionary priest and later bishop. As a dual citizen of the United States and Peru, he’s the first pope from each country.

“My heart is so excited that it makes me want to cry with joy,” said Zuly Castillo, who served as Leo’s secretary when he was bishop of the northern city of Chiclayo near the Pacific Coast. Across from her office, a life-size cardboard cutout of the pope now welcomes visitors to his former residence.

“Peru is the crown of the trip, the homecoming of the first Peruvian pope, no matter where he was born,” said Gustavo Morello, an associate professor of sociology at Boston College and the author of “Lived Religion in Latin America.”

“This is a return to his origins without any doubt,” Morello said.

Under the Saudi sharia law system, sex outside marriage is a criminal offence. But it is women who are disproportionately targeted, say rights groups, which have condemned the punishment as an “act of violence”.
